children.name: Early screen readers worked by scraping video buffers and hooking the drawing calls an app made to the OS. That approach was brittle by construction: it inferred meaning from shapes. A rectangle with text inside might be a button, a tab, or a decorative frame, and the scraper had no way to know. As toolkits moved toward custom-drawn controls, the heuristics broke entirely.

children.name: The fix was to invert responsibility. Instead of assistive technology guessing at intent, the application publishes it. Each element declares a role (button, checkbox, list item), a name, a value, a set of states (focused, disabled, expanded), and its relationships to other elements. Windows shipped MSAA in 1997 and later UI Automation; macOS has NSAccessibility; Linux desktops use AT-SPI; browsers build an equivalent tree from the DOM plus ARIA attributes.

children.name: Hierarchy carries information that a flat list cannot. Containment tells a screen reader that a checkbox lives inside a row, which lives inside a table, which lives inside a dialog — so it can announce "row 3 of 12, Inbox" instead of an orphaned "checked." The hierarchy also drives focus order, hit testing, and grouping, and it lets consumers prune whole subtrees they do not care about.

children.name: Screen readers are the origin story, but the audience is much wider now. Voice control and dictation software need actionable targets. Screen magnifiers follow focus through it. UI test frameworks — Appium, WinAppDriver, Playwright — drive applications through accessibility APIs precisely because they are stable and semantic where coordinates are not. Password managers locate credential fields. And increasingly, automation agents use the tree as a machine-readable interface to software that was only ever designed for human eyes.

children.name: Regulation supplies the pressure. Section 508 in the US, the ADA as applied to software, and EN 301 549 in Europe make accessibility support a procurement requirement rather than a nicety, particularly for anything sold to government or enterprise.

children.name: Mainstream toolkits — Cocoa, WPF, Qt, GTK — populate the tree automatically, so developers using standard widgets get it nearly free. Custom-rendered surfaces do not. Games, canvas-based web apps, and some cross-platform frameworks paint pixels with no semantic layer beneath, which is exactly why they tend to be unusable with assistive technology unless someone builds the tree by hand.
